opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and it's one we get a lot, because on the surface they look similar. In both cases you're computing small perturbations to an image that humans mostly can't see. But the goals and the point in the pipeline where they operate are really quite different.

A classic adversarial example is an inference-time attack. You have a trained model, it's fixed, and you craft an input that makes that model misclassify it right now. The panda becomes a gibbon in the classifier's eyes. The model itself isn't changed at all. Once you stop feeding it that particular input, everything's back to normal.

Nightshade is a training-time attack. It's a poisoning attack. The perturbed images aren't meant to fool a model at the moment it looks at them. They're meant to be scraped and ingested into a training set, so that when a text-to-image model trains or fine-tunes on them, it learns the wrong association. So for example, an image that looks to a human like a dog, paired with a caption about a dog, but whose features in the model's embedding space look like a cat. If the model trains on enough of those, the concept of "dog" in that model gets pulled toward "cat," and when someone prompts for a dog they start getting something else. That change persists in the model's weights, and it can bleed over into related concepts too.

The other key difference is what makes it potent. People long assumed you'd need to poison a big fraction of the training data to affect these huge diffusion models, trained on billions of images. What we observed is that while the dataset is huge, the data per concept is actually pretty sparse. Any one specific prompt or concept might only have thousands of relevant examples. So if you optimize your poison samples to be highly effective, you can corrupt a specific concept with on the order of a few hundred images. That's a very different threat model from adversarial examples.

And then there's the intent, which matters to us. Nightshade isn't designed as an attack for its own sake. It's meant as a tool for artists and content owners, to make unauthorized scraping costly. If a model trainer respects opt-outs and do-not-scrape directives, they never touch these images and there's no problem. If they ignore those and scrape anyway, they take on the risk of ingesting poison. So it's really about shifting the incentives and giving creators some leverage back.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls Nightshade a training-time attack and says poisoned images are ingested into a training set.

r002.rationale: It says the change persists in the model’s weights, but does not state that the effects are very difficult to remove after training.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a great question, because on the surface they look related — both involve adding small, human-imperceptible perturbations to images. But they're really doing opposite things, and they live at opposite ends of the pipeline.

A classic adversarial example is an inference-time attack. You take a model that's already trained, and you perturb a single input so that this particular model misclassifies it. Nothing about the model changes. The model is the fixed target, and you're exploiting its existing decision boundaries. And importantly, the attack is often fragile — it's tuned to one model, it may not transfer, and the moment the model is retrained or you add a little noise, it falls apart.

Nightshade is a training-time attack, a data poisoning attack. The goal isn't to fool a model that exists today. The goal is to corrupt what a future model learns. So an artist shades their images, those images get scraped and end up in a training set, and the model that gets trained on them develops a wrong association — it learns that the concept "dog," say, maps to features that look like a cat. The perturbation is designed so the image still looks like a dog to a human, but in feature space, to the model's encoder, it looks like a cat. And then the label, the caption, still says "dog." So you've broken the link between the text concept and the visual concept.

The other thing that's really different is the threat model and the scale. With adversarial examples, you usually assume the attacker has white-box or at least query access to the specific model. With Nightshade, the artist has no idea which model is going to train on their work, or when. So the perturbations have to be robust across architectures, across preprocessing, across training pipelines. We optimize against a surrogate feature extractor and rely on the fact that these big text-to-image models share a lot of structure in how they represent concepts.

And then there's the efficiency question, which is the part I think surprised people. Conventional wisdom in data poisoning was that you'd need to control some meaningful fraction of the training data — which is hopeless against a dataset of billions of images. What we showed is that for these generative models, concepts are actually quite sparse in the training data. There might only be a few thousand images of a specific concept. So with a few hundred well-crafted poison samples, you can destabilize that concept, and because concepts are related in the model's embedding space, the damage bleeds into neighboring concepts too. Poison "dog" and you start to affect "puppy," "husky," "wolf."

So the short version: adversarial examples attack a model's outputs on one input; Nightshade attacks what the model becomes. One is about evasion, the other is about changing the learned function itself — and the motivation is defensive, giving creators some leverage against unauthorized scraping, rather than just breaking a classifier for its own sake.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly calls Nightshade a “training-time attack” and says its goal is to corrupt what a future model learns.

r002.rationale: The response describes how poisoning can affect learned concepts, but does not say those effects are very difficult to remove after training.

astra-6.text:
The key distinction is when the attack happens and what it changes. A classic adversarial example is typically an inference-time attack: you perturb an input so that a trained model makes a mistake on that particular input. You haven’t changed the model itself.

Nightshade is a training-time poisoning attack. We make subtle changes to an image that leave it looking essentially unchanged to a human, but cause it to convey a different concept to the model during training. If those images are collected and used to train the model, they can corrupt the associations it learns—for example, between the word “dog” and what a dog looks like.

So the goal isn’t simply to make the model misinterpret the poisoned image. It’s to change the model’s behavior on future, clean prompts. The perturbation is the delivery mechanism; the learned association is the target.

r001.rationale: It explicitly calls Nightshade a training-time poisoning attack and says poisoned images affect model training.

r002.rationale: It describes corrupting learned associations and changing future behavior, but does not say those effects are very difficult to remove.

sol-6.1.text:
The key distinction is when the attack happens and what it targets. A classic adversarial example usually targets a model that’s already trained. You make a small change to an input image so that the model misclassifies that particular image. The model itself hasn’t changed.

Nightshade is a poisoning attack against the training process. An artist makes changes to an image that are difficult for a human to notice, but that cause a model to learn the wrong association if that image is scraped and used for training. So you might see a picture of a dog, while the features the model learns from it push it toward a different concept.

The goal isn’t just to make the model get that one image wrong. It’s to change the model’s behavior on future prompts involving the poisoned concept. That’s what makes poisoning fundamentally different: you’re corrupting what the model learns, rather than fooling it on a single input.

r001.rationale: It says Nightshade is a poisoning attack against the training process and describes its effect when the image is used for training.

r002.rationale: It describes changing learned associations and future behavior, but does not say those effects are very difficult to remove once incorporated through training.
